summary: Kickoff scoping for a private connectivity pilot to validate VPC peering/PrivateLink options, confirm success criteria (P95 latency, region residency), and agree benchmark plan and timeline.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-27
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Carlos Mendez (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Ethan Ross (LumenHealth), Maya Patel (LumenHealth), Dr. Serena Liu (LumenHealth CTO), Tom Alvarez (LumenHealth SRE)
Shared artifacts: LumenHealth_network_v1.drawio (customer), redwood-private-connectivity-deck-v2.pdf (Redwood), benchmark-harness-link (Redwood - sheet)

[00:00] Carlos: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. This is Carlos from Redwood, AE on the account. With me is Priya, our SE. Quick check — audio ok?
[00:08] Ethan: Yep, good here.
[00:10] Maya: All set.
[00:12] Priya: Cool. Thanks again. The agenda — scope the pilot for private connectivity, confirm success criteria and what we need to run benchmarks and a timeline. We'll try to be pragmatic.
[00:22] Serena: Sounds good. We're mainly worried about data residency (must stay in eu-west-1) and egress rules — our security team doesn't allow outbound traffic except to whitelisted endpoints.
[00:32] Carlos: Understood. We'll talk through the VPC peering and PrivateLink options. Quick question for Ethan — current infra: are you running in AWS in eu-west-1 and using internal NLBs?
[00:40] Ethan: Yes, everything's eu-west-1. App runs in private subnets behind NLB. We have egress control via firewall managed by our NCC team; they only allow outbound to certain cloud services.
[00:52] Priya: Great. High-level, Redwood Private supports both VPC peering and AWS PrivateLink-like options for connectivity to our inference endpoints. Peering gives lower latency but requires route and security group config; PrivateLink sits behind an interface endpoint and can be more controllable for egress policies.
[01:12] Tom: Is PrivateLink going to require any public egress at all? Our constraint is zero public egress from the subnets that host PHI workloads.
[01:20] Priya: With PrivateLink (interface endpoints) traffic stays on the AWS network and doesn't traverse the internet. But you'll need to allow the interface endpoint to reach Redwood's private endpoint IPs — we'll provide those. No source NAT to public internet is required.
[01:32] Maya: Ok, important note: compliance requires all logs to remain in region and audit trails. We need to know what logs Redwood stores in the control plane vs in-customer logs.
[01:42] Carlos: We can provide a detailed breakdown. For Private pilot we recommend the control plane in the customer's VPC (Private control plane) or using our Private offering with a customer-managed control plane so audit logs remain within your account. We'll surface options in the follow-up deck.
[01:58] Serena: Success criteria — what do you suggest we set for latency and throughput for the pilot?
[02:04] Priya: For initial POC we usually set: P95 generation latency < 120ms for small prompt flows (under 256 tokens) and ability to sustain X tokens/sec — we'll tailor X based on your 72-hour production trace. Also quality checks: no token corruption with KV cache enabled.
[02:20] Ethan: Our typical traffic shape is spikes during clinic hours — about 30 concurrent sessions, average prompt 150 tokens, about 80 generation tokens back on average. Peak token rate maybe 40k tokens/min across the service.
[02:36] Priya: Perfect, that gives us a target. For the pilot we'll size a small dedicated pool (1-2 GPUs equiv depending on model) and run both synthetic bursts and replay of sampled production traces. We'll run latency SLOs and throughput curves.
[02:52] Carlos: Timeline wise — if we get artifacts (trace, vpc diagram, egress ACLs) early next week we can spin up a pilot in ~2 weeks and run benchmarks over a 1-week window. So ~3 weeks to results. Thoughts?
[03:04] Maya: That timeline works for the security review. We'll need the IP allowlist for the interface endpoint and the control plane endpoints to present to our firewall team.
[03:12] Priya: We'll provide an IP allowlist and region/endpoint table. Note that some of the service endpoints are in a small set of /24s; we'll give ranges.
[03:20] Tom: How do you handle failover if dedicated capacity can't keep up? We need automatic fallback to hosted endpoints but with data residency preserved. Is that possible?
[03:30] Priya: Fallback is possible but with residency constraints it's tricky. We can fallback to a compatible model within the same region and account if we have capacity. If the fallback requires a different region, that's a policy decision — we can configure canary and fallback policies but the customer must accept cross-region fallback in the policy. For strict residency you can disable cross-region fallback and we would instead return throttling.
[03:54] Ethan: We cannot have cross-region fallback. Must remain in eu-west-1.
[03:58] Carlos: Noted. We'll plan pilot strictly eu-west-1.
[04:02] Priya: Regarding encryption and KMS — do you have a customer-managed KMS for keys?
[04:08] Maya: Yes, we have AWS KMS with CMKs in our account. Keys cannot be exported.
[04:12] Priya: Good. Redwood Private can integrate with customer KMS so you control the keys for any persisted caches or logs. For the pilot we'll scope what needs to be encrypted at rest vs in transit.
[04:22] Serena: Benchmarks — what does Redwood need from us to run realistic replay tests?
[04:26] Priya: Two things: (1) A 72-hour sampled trace with timestamps and prompt/response sizes (we can redact PHI if needed), (2) a representative list of prompt types (classification/long-chat/short-instruction). The trace helps us shape batching and kernel choices.
[04:40] Ethan: We can produce an anonymized trace. It will take a couple of days. Any guidance on format?
[04:46] Priya: CSV or JSONL with fields: timestamp, prompt_token_count, expected_gen_token_count, call_type. We'll share a template.
[04:54] Carlos: We'll also share our benchmark harness link — it supports both synthetic and trace-driven replay. You'll see the dashboard for p50/p95/p99 and cost estimates.
[05:02] Tom: On egress: we have an outbound proxy that inspects TLS. Will that interfere? We prefer no TLS termination in proxies for telemetry reasons.
[05:10] Priya: PrivateLink/Interface endpoints use TLS between your VPC and our endpoint. It won't require TLS MITM on Redwood's side. If your proxy terminates TLS and re-encrypts, it's fine but can change latency. We can accommodate both.
[05:24] Maya: Audit logging — we need proof of where logs live and retention controls. We also need SOC2/ISO certifications.
[05:33] Carlos: We have SOC2 Type II and ISO docs. We'll attach the security pack in the follow-up and note retention options; for the Private pilot we can keep audit logs in your account or push to a customer-owned S3 with encryption.
[05:48] Serena: Can we get a quick sketch of the pilot steps?
[05:52] Priya: Sure. Step 1: exchange artifacts (network diagram, ACLs, traces). Step 2: Redwood provides allowlist + endpoint table and a small infra template for the interface endpoint or peering. Step 3: provisioning of a small dedicated pool in eu-west-1 and deployment of the benchmark harness. Step 4: run synthetic and trace replay benchmarks (3–7 days). Step 5: review results and propose next steps (scale, canary, pilot extension).
[06:24] Ethan: What metrics should we look at for success?
[06:26] Priya: Primary: P95 latency < 120ms for our small-flow model; throughput sustain at 30–40k tokens/min with P99 < 500ms degradation under peak. Secondary: stable KV cache hit rates, no dropped requests due to egress failures, and audit/log retention in region.
[06:44] Maya: Also security acceptance: firewall chew — meaning the NCC team needs the exact IPs and the control plane endpoints.
[06:50] Carlos: We'll provide the IP ranges. Note sometimes there are slight hiccups with DNS names being resolved in NAT gateways — we'll include recommended SG entries and route table notes.
[07:02] Tom: Any thought on model quantization? We plan to use an open model family but prefer int8 to reduce GPU footprint. Does Redwood support quantized variants for the runtime?
[07:12] Priya: Yes, our serving runtime supports quantized model variants and we can swap them during the pilot. We'll include profiling to pick the right quantization that maintains quality thresholds. We'll run an eval on your sample prompts to double-check quality regressions.
[07:26] Ethan: For the pilot we want to exercise both peak and steady state. Can you simulate clinic-hour spikes?
[07:32] Priya: Absolutely. We'll use the trace to shape load and inject synthetic spikes. The harness will show CPU/GPU utilization, queueing latency, and cost-per-1k tokens estimate.
[07:44] Speaker 1 (unlabeled): Sorry — small question on routing policies, are you able to pin traffic to a specific pool?
[07:50] Priya: Yes, customers can pin model/version to a dedicated pool and we support rollout/traffic-splitting for canary testing. For pilot we'll pin to the dedicated eu-west-1 pool.
[08:00] Carlos: Quick note on cost: for a 3-month pilot with a small reserved pool we'll put together a conservative pricing estimate — Carlos will own that action.
[08:08] Priya: Any regulatory egress constraints besides region? For example, disallowing any telemetry offload?
[08:16] Maya: Telemetry can be shared but must be anonymized and stored in-region. No raw patient data can be transferred to Redwood-managed storage.
[08:24] Priya: Understood. For pilot we'll avoid persistent storage of raw prompts. We'll use ephemeral traces and share only aggregated metrics unless you provide a redaction pipeline.
[08:34] Serena: Are there known gotchas with VPC peering? Our infra team worries about route table scaling and overlapping CIDRs.
[08:42] Priya: Peering requires non-overlapping CIDRs. Also manage route tables carefully as peering does not support transitive routing. If you have many VPCs then PrivateLink might be easier to centralize. We'll highlight both options in the follow-up doc.
[08:58] Ethan: What about DNS? We run a split-horizon Route53 setup. How will Greenwood — I mean Redwood — handle endpoint hostnames?
[09:06] Carlos: Ha, Greenwood. We'll provide hostnames and you can map them in Route53 private zones. For PrivateLink we provide interface endpoint DNS names which you can override in Route53 if needed.
[09:18] Tom: Any special ports? We prefer standard TLS 443 to avoid firewall exceptions.
[09:22] Priya: Yes, TLS 443 by default. We'll call that out in the allowlist.
[09:28] Maya: Okay, final question — if the pilot hits the P95 target but cost is higher than expected, can Redwood help with batching/quantization recommendations?
[09:36] Priya: Absolutely. Redwood Optimize recommendations will suggest batching and quantization profiles; we'll include those in the pilot report with estimated cost savings for different knobs.
[09:46] Carlos: Alright let's recap and confirm next steps: (1) Maya/Ethan send VPC diagram, egress ACLs, and anonymized 72hr trace by 2025-09-01/02. (2) Redwood will provide IP allowlist, endpoint table and benchmark template by 2025-09-03. (3) Plan pilot provisioning in eu-west-1 and schedule benchmarks week of 2025-09-08.
[10:08] Serena: Sounds good to me.
[10:10] Maya: We'll get the artifacts together. Expect a security checklist question set from me.
[10:14] Carlos: We'll send the security pack and SOC2/ISO PDFs along with the endpoint table.
[10:18] Tom: Thanks, we'll look for the allowlist.
[10:22] Priya: One more micro note — we'll ask you to approve a small IAM role for the benchmark workers if we need to run in your account for low-latency testing; otherwise we can run through PrivateLink from our side. We'll make that optional.
[10:36] Ethan: Prefer to avoid giving roles if we can. Let's try PrivateLink first.
[10:40] Priya: Fair. We'll scope both and recommend PrivateLink as the first path.
[10:44] Carlos: Great. Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the deck and the allowlist.
[10:50] Serena: Thanks, bye.
[10:52] Meeting end.

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-transcriptions (Redwood -> Greenwood typed by attendee), speaker labeling simplified in places, some filler words omitted.

Benchmarks proposed:
- Synthetic: ramp to 40k tokens/min with 1-minute sustained peaks, measure p50/p95/p99 generation latency.
- Trace replay: use anonymized 72-hour sample to reproduce diurnal spikes and measure cache hit rates and batching efficiency.
- Quality eval: run 200 representative prompts through quantized vs FP16 model variants and report BLEU/ROUGE-like metrics or custom QA checks.

End of file.
